title: Arms and Artefacts
text: Arms and Artefacts The objects of the Obligatory Quest: swords above fireplaces, hats required by forms, benches in eleven pieces, and one crate, stencilled on all six faces, which you should not have opened. The full catalogue is in preparation.

title: Bestiary
text: Bestiary The creatures of the road, as reported by the people they were rude to. I have not met any of them myself and do not intend to. I have relied, for the classification, on Wren Halloway, who has, and who will tell you what they are whether you have asked or not. The full catalogue is in preparation.

title: A Glossary of Cliches
text: A Glossary of Cliches An adventuring convention is a thing that happens on every quest because it happened on the first one, and nobody has thought to stop it. The Forty-Eighth walked into very nearly all of them. This volume lists them, with where he walked into each, and who was still annoyed about it. The glossary is in preparation.

title: History
text: History The history of the world, so far as anyone has written it down, is very largely the history of one document. Everything before the Prophecy of Thistlewick belongs to the elves, who will tell you about it if you ask and who have never been asked. Everything since belongs to the Prophecy, which has been asked a great deal and has answered, every time, in clauses. This volume holds the articles that are about time rather than about a person or a place. Article What it covers The Prophecy of Thistlewick The document itself: its signing, its clauses, and what it turned out to be. The Chosen Ones All forty-eight of them, so far as they are known, with what became of each. The Obligatory Quest The quest of the Forty-Eighth, from the bed to the throne room, and after. Two Reckonings Why the Tower is two thousand years old and four thousand eight hundred, and both are true. Timeline Every date I could pin, in order.

title: The Thistle-pedia
text: The Thistle-pedia Being Volume Three of A Complete And Accurate History Of The Obligatory Quest , arranged alphabetically so that people will stop coming to my table to ask me things. The compiler, at work. The hand at the temple is thought. The ink on it is also thought, after a fashion. My name is Hosea Bellwether , and I am the historian of the Obligatory Quest. I am not the only historian of the Obligatory Quest - the Prophecy Committee of Thistlewick keeps minutes, and the minutes are very thorough about biscuits - but I am the only one who has ever gone and asked the people it happened to. I do my asking from a table of my own by the fire in the Slain Wyvern , in Nether Sopping , where the book lives. It needs a table of its own. You will understand why when you try to lift it. This is the third volume. Volume One was a pamphlet, and there is still a copy upstairs in the Wyvern for any guest who finds themselves short of something to read and long on time. Volume Two is downstairs and is the size of a door; it has been mistaken for one, twice, by people coming in out of the rain. This volume is the same history again, cut up into articles and put in order, with pictures, so that you may look up a turnip farmer, a goose or a clause of a contract without having to read the four hundred pages in between. The compiler I should say at the outset that I have never been on a quest. That is the qualification. Everybody else in the Slain Wyvern has been on one, and not one of them would tell a historian about it - they told me about the weather, and their knees, and what Thistlewick charges for a pint. So for a long while my great work was complete , in the sense that it had a beginning and an end and a great many chapters in the middle, and it was not accurate , in the sense that nobody in it had been consulted. Then, in the year 2000, a young man from Thistlewick came in out of the wet with a sword he did not seem entirely comfortable holding, and stood about. I wrote him down at once. Chapter Three Hundred and Twelve: The Forty-Eighth arrives, and stands about. It remains, I think, the most accurate sentence in the history, and he read it over my shoulder and did not dispute it. His name was Bram Thistle . He was the forty-eighth Chosen One of the Prophecy of Thistlewick , a turnip farmer by trade, and the Prophecy Committee had chosen him while he was asleep. I asked him to do the one thing I could not: to go round the room and be told . Six first-hand accounts, heard properly, to the end. He did. Nobody does. They get two and go and look at a dungeon. He got six, and came back, and I paid him handsomely for a man with ink on both hands, and I wrote him into the history in small type at the bottom of page four hundred and one. The footnote says that he listened. Nobody else has one. Then I told him to go north, and that I would leave the last page blank until I heard how it went, and that coming back to tell me was the fee. He came back. He paid. This book is what he paid for. That was two years ago, near enough, and in the two years since I have gone round again and asked everybody what became of them afterwards, which is a question nobody in the Slain Wyvern had ever been asked either. Their answers are at the end of their articles. The world, briefly It is a small world and a long one, and most of it is weather. * Thistlewick * is a village in the middle of it which believes, sincerely and on paper, that it is the middle of it. Every hundred years - or every hundred years as the Committee reckons them, which is a separate subject and has its own article - the Dark Lord rises in the Obligatory Tower to the north, and Thistlewick sends a Chosen One to put him down. It has worked forty-seven times. Thistlewick is extremely proud of this, and has never once asked why there is always a next time. * Nether Sopping *, where I am writing this, is a wet fishing town on the south coast, forty miles from Thistlewick and the better part of a world away. It is where Thistlewick's Chosen Ones go when they come back, under clause nineteen , which gives a returning hero a pension, a cottage and "such distance from the village as is mutually agreeable". The distance turns out to be forty miles, and the agreement turns out to be Thistlewick's. As a consequence every adventurer in the world who has finished adventuring has pooled down here, in one tavern, with their old companions, their old grudges and a stuffed wyvern over the mantel which is a goose. The north belongs to Upper Clanging , a town of engineers who have been trying for two hundred years to build a ship that flies to the Tower, and to the Long Field , where they keep the ones that did not. Further north still there is snow, and Frostwick , and a chapter house that has filed everything. The west has Great Dunnage , a city of guilds, and in the south-west the elves of Olde Evermore , who have been here longer than the calendar and are very nice about it. The east has a magical college and a village that was flooded in somebody's absence, and the south-east a great house whose portraits watch you. And above all of it, on a cloud, there is a castle that nobody has ever reached, with a caretaker in it, who has been waiting. There are, besides, a great many standing stones, wells, signposts, hermits, chests and old men who know things. I have tried to give each of them their due. Some of them have asked me not to. What happened What happened, to put it as shortly as I am able - and I am not, by temperament, able - is that the Forty-Eighth went north, as forty-seven had before him, and climbed the Tower, and met the Dark Lord, and found that the Dark Lord did not want to be there either. Grimspite the Inevitable had held the post for four thousand eight hundred years, by the Prophecy's own count, under a contract that renewed itself every time a hero beat him. He had been beaten forty-seven times, and every time it had counted as a renewal. The Prophecy, you see, was never a prophecy. It was an employment contract, and it had a clause twelve, and when the Forty-Eighth beat him the contract itself unrolled to enforce it. The Forty-Eighth beat that as well. You may read about it under The Obligatory Quest , and about clause twelve under The Prophecy of Thistlewick . Thistlewick struck clause twelve from its records afterwards and wrote in its place a note reading SEE BRAM. Nobody has needed to yet. Six months later, after a very long meeting, it struck clause nineteen as well. He did not go alone. He went with friends - a healer, a smith, a hedge mage, a shopkeeper, a knight, a bard, a brooding man, a naturalist, a guest star and, in the end, a boy from a boiler - though never with all of them at once, and which three of them climbed the last stair with him depends on whom you ask, and everybody I asked says it was them. I have given all of them articles. I have not adjudicated. A historian who adjudicates between a blacksmith and a knight about who was standing nearest the Dark Lord does not remain a historian for long. He becomes a footnote, in somebody else's book, in small type. How to use this book The volumes are these: Volume What is in it History The Prophecy and its clauses; the forty-eight Chosen Ones; the Quest of the Forty-Eighth; the two calendars and why they disagree; a timeline. People The Forty-Eighth and his companions; the Dark Lord; and the people of the towns, villages and holes in the ground. Places Every settlement, ruin, tower and tavern I have been able to visit, write to or hear about. Institutions The Prophecy Committee, the Adventurers' Guild (Provisional), the Hoyle Works, the Collegium Arcanum and other bodies with minutes. Bestiary The creatures of the road, with notes on which of them are what they say they are. Arms and Artefacts Swords, hats, benches and one crate, stencilled on all six faces. A Glossary of Cliches The well-worn conventions of the adventuring life, as the Forty-Eighth walked into very nearly all of them. Words in a different colour lead to other articles. Words in red lead to articles I have promised and not yet written; I am told this is normal in an encyclopedia and I find it a great comfort. The box at the top of the page will search the whole work, which is more than I can do with Volume Two. A word on accuracy Everything in this book is complete. Not all of it is accurate. Where my sources agree, I have said so. Where they disagree I have given both sides, or all eleven, and said which I believe and why, and you may believe the other. Where they cannot both be true - Merrow Halgate's account of the bridge and Councillor Dree's account of the chair, for instance, cannot both be true on a Tuesday - I have printed both, because that is what complete means. Where nobody knows, I have said that nobody knows, and then, being human, I have usually guessed, and marked the guess as mine. I have been asked by the Prophecy Committee to make clear that this work is not authorised by the Prophecy Committee. It is not. I have also been asked by the elves of Olde Evermore to make clear that the Third Age did not begin with the Prophecy. I asked them what it did begin with, and Elder Faelan said that it began with a great many things, and that the Prophecy was the one with a clerk present. I have left it there. So, I think, should you. Acknowledgements To the regulars of the Slain Wyvern, who told me nothing for years and then told the Forty-Eighth everything in a fortnight. To Dorcas Thrupp, for the table. To the goose. To Piper Quill, who was also writing it all down, and whose version has more rhymes in it and fewer footnotes, and whom I consider a colleague and, in the matter of scansion, a rival. And to Bram Thistle, Chosen One Number Forty-Eight, who came back and told me how it went - all of it, in order, including the part about the tea - and so paid the fee. H. B. The Slain Wyvern, Nether Sopping The twenty-first of March, Third Age 2002, which Spare Cotterill has confirmed by letter is spring

title: Institutions
text: Institutions An institution is a group of people who have agreed to keep minutes. The world has a great many of them, and the minutes are where most of my evidence comes from, which is to say that my evidence is very thorough about biscuits. Institution Seat The Prophecy Committee Prophecy Hall, Thistlewick The Adventurers' Guild (Provisional) Nether Sopping The Hoyle Works Upper Clanging The Collegium Arcanum the east, since 1400

title: People
text: People A great many people have been on the Obligatory Quest, and a great many more have stood beside the road while it went past. This volume holds the ones who did something about it - which in practice means the ones who talked to me, or to the Forty-Eighth, which is the same thing at one remove. The Forty-Eighth and his company Bram Thistle Merribell Hob Grumnir Zephyrine Vance Nix Sir Aldric Piper Quill Corvin Ash Wren Halloway Roland Fairweather Spare Cotterill The other party to the contract Grimspite the Inevitable , the Dark Lord, retired Everybody else The people of the towns are being written up a town at a time, and are listed here as each town is done. Hosea Bellwether , the compiler, who was persuaded that leaving himself out would be inaccurate

title: Places
text: Places The world is about a hundred and twenty days' walk across in either direction, by the reckoning of anyone who has tried it, and most of those days are spent in a field. What follows are the parts that are not field. The road north Place What it is Thistlewick The village that sends the Chosen Ones, and believes itself the middle of the world. Firstfield Meadow A meadow at the foot of a rainbow, where things are explained to you. The Gloamwood A wood, with a Thing in it, and a man on a log. The Obligatory Tower Where the Dark Lord lives. Ground floor. Door at the bottom. The south Place What it is Nether Sopping Where the Chosen Ones go afterwards. The sea is right there. The Slain Wyvern A tavern, with a goose over the mantel. Also, my table. The Lighthouse of Saint Bother A light for a sea nobody sails. The Bottomless Pit Approximately. The Barrow of the Forty-Fourth A hero's grave, with a bench on it. The north Place What it is Upper Clanging Engineers, rain, and a ship two hundred years in the making. The Long Field Where Upper Clanging keeps its attempts. Frostwick Snow, a working group, and the only person who has read clause two. Further out The rest of the world is being written up as I am able to visit it, or as people come in out of the rain and tell me about it. It includes Great Dunnage , Olde Evermore and a great many villages with fewer than one inn.
